new_statements.translation: As a supra-segmental element there is, for example, tone. Given that Bankon is a tone language, a study of the tones that play a distinctive role in this language will be undertaken, following the paradigmatic and syntagmatic axes as well.

Etant donne que le ɓàŋkón est une langue à tons, une etude des tons qui jouent un role distinctif dans cette langue sera envisagee, et suivant aussi les deux axes paradigmatique et syntagmatique." The only difference from the reported quote is the spelling of the language name: the page writes it with implosive b-hook and eng (ɓàŋkón), the report norm…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bankon is described as a tone language with five tonemes (low, mid, high, rising, falling); the source says nothing about word stress or a culminative accent. The only 'accent' remark (p. 75) concerns English loanwords whose H-B tone melody is attributed to English initial stress, which implies stress is not a native Bankon category in this author's analysis but is not stated as such.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. p. 75: the H-B tonal sequence on disyllables is rare in native words (about 6/1400) and found mainly in English loans (bótà 'butter', sóndʒà 'soldier', drósì 'dress', kótì 'coatee', kótìn 'cotton'), explained by the stressed first syllable of the English source.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (lexemes and noun/verb stems, citation forms); no phrase-level stress discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Atindogbé 1990 describes the Bankon dialect proper (spoken north of the Wouri estuary, Dibombari, Moungo), which ALCAM treats as one of two dialects (bankon, lombe) of a language it calls 'lombe' — hence the thesis subtitle '(dialecte lombe)'. Glottolog bank1256 = Bankon/Abo [abb]; the sister lect Lombe/Barombi is baro1252 [bbi]. Hyman & Lionnet 2011 call the same language Abo (A42).

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (Atindogbe 1990): tonal, no stress statement. Spellenberg 1922 is compatible (he also describes lexical/grammatical tone, par. 19-20) and ADDS a stress statement: predictable stress on the stem (root) syllable, unmarked. Nothing on record contradicts this; combined picture = tone language with root-syllable (stem-initial) dynamic stress per the 1922 primary description. Source quality caveat: snippet-level evidence from three digitisations of the same text; a hand download of HathiTrust uva.x001506363 p. 25 (or mdp.39015050687709, Beiheft 3 p. 25, shortly before seq 361) would upgrade it to a page-verified quote.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Spellenberg (with Meinhof) treats Bankon as a tone language (par. 19 Tonzeichen, par. 20 Zur Tonlehre: high/low tone, incl. grammatical tone such as a bon 'he gives' vs. 'he has given') and states separately that the dynamic (stress) accent always lies on the stem syllable -- i.e. the root syllable, not the class/concord prefixes -- and, being fully predictable, is left unmarked in the transcription.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the visible text (par. 21 is a single sentence).
new_statements.exceptions: none: 'immer' (always) on the stem syllable; no exceptions visible in the snippet. Caveat: read from search snippets, not from a page view; a footnote or following remark cannot be fully excluded, though the snippet runs straight on into 'Formenlehre'.
new_statements.identity_note: Spellenberg 1922 describes Bo/Bankon (Abo), Bantu A42, Cameroon (Basel Mission field, Littoral); the catalog source Atindogbé 1990 describes the Lombe dialect of Bankon.

sources.note: Whole thesis is a structuralist phonology (tones, vowels, consonants, syllable/word structure). States p. 13 that Bankon is a tone language ('le bànkón est une langue à tons') and inventories five tonemes (bas, moyen, haut, montant, descendant, pp. 14-16). Contains no statement on word stress/accent in Bankon; the only mention of 'accent' (p. 75) is that the rare H-B tonal sequence occurs mostly in English loanwords (bótà 'butter', sóndʒà 'soldier') and is attributed to English initial stress. Verified against page scan (pp. 18 and 80).
